description: Manchuria, Abyssinia, Rhineland, Sudetenland — the League's failures and the road to war.
content_html:
The 1930s: From Crisis to Crisis

The 1930s saw the international order constructed at Paris and developed through the Locarno agreements come under sustained assault. Each successive crisis — Manchuria, Abyssinia, the Rhineland, Anschluss, the Sudetenland — tested the League and the policy of appeasement, and each test revealed further weaknesses. An important examiner’s note: stay within the correct time-frames. Manchuria and Abyssinia are 1930s crises; do not mix them with 1920s events such as Corfu or Vilna.

Key Fact

Key timeline: Manchuria (1931), Abyssinia invaded (October 1935), Rhineland remilitarised (March 1936), Anschluss with Austria (March 1938), Munich Agreement over the Sudetenland (September 1938), Nazi-Soviet Pact (23 August 1939), Germany invades Poland (1 September 1939), Britain and France declare war (3 September 1939).

The Abyssinian Crisis 1935–1936

In October 1935, Mussolini’s Italy invaded Abyssinia (now Ethiopia), one of only two independent African nations. The League responded by imposing economic sanctions on Italy — a significant step, the first time sanctions had been applied against a major power. However, the sanctions excluded oil, coal, and steel, the resources Italy most needed to sustain military operations. Britain and France also negotiated the secret Hoare-Laval Pact, which proposed giving Mussolini most of the territory he sought in exchange for peace; the plan leaked and caused a political scandal, forcing both foreign ministers to resign.

Italy completed its conquest of Abyssinia by May 1936. The League lifted its sanctions the same month. The crisis had multiple consequences: it demonstrated that the League could impose sanctions but not make them effective without full participation; it pushed Mussolini towards closer alignment with Hitler; and it revealed the lengths to which Britain and France would go to avoid confrontation with a major power.

Hitler’s Challenges to Versailles

Adolf Hitler came to power explicitly committed to overturning the Versailles settlement. He moved methodically through a series of unilateral actions, each one testing whether Britain and France would respond with force. In March 1935, he publicly announced the existence of a German air force (forbidden at Versailles) and reintroduced conscription. The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June 1935, under which Britain allowed Germany a navy up to 35 per cent of the Royal Navy’s tonnage, appeared to accept German rearmament without demanding equivalent concessions.

In March 1936, German troops remilitarised the Rhineland — a direct violation of both the Versailles Treaty and the Locarno Treaties, which Germany had voluntarily signed in 1925. France had the legal right to respond militarily. However, neither France nor Britain took action. French military commanders argued they needed full mobilisation to respond, which the government was unwilling to order; British leaders believed Germany had legitimate grievances and that a remilitarised Rhineland was not a cause for war. The failure to respond encouraged Hitler to believe that bolder moves would also go unchallenged.

In March 1938, German troops crossed into Austria and Hitler announced the Anschluss — the union of Germany and Austria. This directly violated the Versailles settlement, which had expressly forbidden such a merger. Britain and France again took no military action, though they formally protested. Many Austrians welcomed unification, which complicated any argument that Germany was simply a straightforward aggressor.

The Sudetenland crisis of 1938 followed a similar pattern but on a larger stage. The Sudetenland was a region of Czechoslovakia with a large ethnic German population. Hitler demanded its transfer to Germany, claiming the German minority faced persecution. Britain and France, led by Chamberlain and Daladier, negotiated the Munich Agreement of September 1938, transferring the Sudetenland to Germany without consulting Czechoslovakia. Chamberlain returned to London claiming to have secured “peace for our time.” In March 1939, German troops occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia, demonstrating that the Munich Agreement had been worthless.

The Policy of Appeasement

Appeasement has been assessed in sharply contrasting ways by historians. The traditional “Guilty Men” view, popularised in 1940 by a pamphlet written by Michael Foot and others, presented Chamberlain and his colleagues as naive fools who fed a crocodile hoping to be eaten last. This interpretation dominated British political memory for a generation.

From the 1960s, revisionist historians led by A.J.P. Taylor and later R.A.C. Parker have offered more nuanced readings. Taylor argued in The Origins of the Second World War (1961) that Hitler was an opportunist rather than a long-term planner, and that Western statesmen made reasonable decisions given their information. Parker acknowledged British public opinion was strongly against another war in the 1930s, that rearmament was not yet complete, and that Chamberlain’s options were more limited than his critics allowed. Most contemporary historians present appeasement as a defensible policy in 1936–37 that became increasingly untenable as Hitler’s aggression escalated beyond revisionist demands into outright conquest.

Key Fact

The “Guilty Men” interpretation condemns Chamberlain as naive and morally culpable for trusting Hitler. The revisionist interpretation (Parker) argues Chamberlain faced genuine constraints — an incomplete rearmament programme, public hostility to war, and the need to buy time — and made reasonable choices given the information available to him. Both views are assessed at the top band for interpretation questions.

The Nazi-Soviet Pact and the Outbreak of War

The Nazi-Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939 shocked Western governments. The ideological enemies of fascism and communism had concluded a non-aggression agreement, and its secret protocol divided Eastern Europe between them. Stalin had been negotiating with Britain and France for a mutual security agreement through the summer of 1939, but grew frustrated at the slow pace of talks and the absence of a genuine military commitment. His decision to align with Germany eliminated the threat of a two-front war for Hitler.

On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Britain and France, having given Poland a guarantee in March 1939, declared war on 3 September. The Second World War had begun — though historians continue to debate how far the Versailles settlement, the Depression, the failures of appeasement, or Hitler’s personal ideology were the decisive causes.

It is tempting to draw a straight line from the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 to the outbreak of war in 1939. Some historians, following the Keynes tradition, argue the punitive reparations and humiliating war guilt clause created resentment that Hitler exploited. However, this single-cause explanation does not account for the Depression’s role in radicalising German politics, the specific choices made by Western leaders during appeasement, or the decisions Hitler himself took. The examiner’s concern noted in this unit’s teaching brief is precisely this: students describe the road to war as inevitable when historians do not agree that it was. Presenting the evidence for multiple causes, and acknowledging historians’ disagreement about their relative weight, is what the top band rewards.
exam_tip_html: Time-frame discipline is essential in this lesson. Manchuria and Abyssinia are 1930s crises; Corfu and Vilna are 1920s. A common error flagged in examiner reports is offering Marshall Aid or the Truman Doctrine as examples of 1930s events — these belong to the late 1940s. For appeasement questions, ensure you can present both the “Guilty Men” condemnation and the revisionist (Parker) defence. For the Munich Agreement specifically: name the four parties (Britain, France, Germany, Italy), note that Czechoslovakia was excluded, and note that Chamberlain returned claiming “peace for our time.” The Nazi-Soviet Pact is examinable: name both the public element (non-aggression) and the secret protocol (dividing Eastern Europe).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The League of Nations failed its major tests in the 1930s: sanctions on Italy over Abyssinia were too partial to work, and the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in 1936 went unchallenged despite violating both Versailles and Locarno.
  • The policy of appeasement, most associated with Chamberlain, culminated in the Munich Agreement of September 1938; revisionist historians such as Parker argue Chamberlain faced genuine constraints, while the “Guilty Men” tradition condemns his judgement as a catastrophic failure.
  • The Nazi-Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939 cleared the way for the German invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939, triggering declarations of war by Britain and France on 3 September.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the Abyssinian crisis of 1935-1936 damaged the League of Nations.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each way scores 1 mark for identification and 1 for specific detail. Examples: sanctions excluded key resources such as oil and coal (1), meaning they failed to halt Italy's military campaign (1); the secret Hoare-Laval Pact (1) proposed rewarding Italy with most of Abyssinia and caused a major political scandal when it leaked (1); Italy completed the conquest of Abyssinia and the League lifted sanctions (1), demonstrating it could not enforce collective security against a major power (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Britain and France did not prevent Germany from remilitarising the Rhineland in March 1936.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed — French military argued full mobilisation was required and the government was unwilling to order it; British leaders believed Germany had legitimate grievances about Versailles and were not willing to go to war over German troops entering German territory. Each reason connected to the outcome (failure to act). Secure: Both explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained, one named. Emerging: Reference to not acting without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Munich Agreement of September 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature plus 1 mark for detail. Feature 1: Britain, France, Germany and Italy agreed to transfer the Sudetenland to Germany (1); Czechoslovakia was not consulted about the decision (1). Feature 2: Chamberlain returned to Britain claiming it secured 'peace for our time' (1); in March 1939 Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia, proving the agreement had failed (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the policy of appeasement failed to prevent the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Multiple causes explained — each concession encouraged further demands rather than satisfying Hitler; the Munich Agreement demonstrated that threats of force without follow-through were ineffective; Hitler's aims went beyond revising Versailles to continental domination; the Nazi-Soviet Pact removed the constraint of a two-front war. Secure: Two or more causes explained. Developing: One cause explained, others listed. Emerging: General statement about appeasement failing without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of the policy of appeasement. Interpretation A (the 'Guilty Men' view) argues Chamberlain and his colleagues made disastrous and avoidable mistakes by trusting Hitler. Interpretation B (the revisionist view) argues Chamberlain faced genuine constraints and made defensible decisions given the information available to him. How far do these interpretations differ and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear identification of key differences (moral verdict vs. contextual judgement; hindsight vs. contemporary knowledge); uses own knowledge (incomplete rearmament, public hostility to war, Munich concessions, March 1939 occupation) to support each; explains reasons for disagreement (era of writing, what evidence each weights). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Notes differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was appeasement the main cause of the Second World War? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs appeasement (Rhineland non-response, Munich) against other causes (Depression and rise of Nazism, Versailles grievances, Nazi-Soviet Pact, Hitler's ideology); engages with named interpretations ('Guilty Men', Parker's revisionism); reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: Clear argument addressing appeasement and at least two other factors with specific evidence. Developing: Some argument, possibly focused only on appeasement or only on Hitler. Emerging: Descriptive account of events. SPaG: 5 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: Which secret plan proposed giving Mussolini most of Abyssinia, causing a major political scandal when it leaked?
In which month and year was the Rhineland remilitarised?
The union of Germany and Austria proclaimed by Hitler in March 1938 was called the _____.
The Nazi-Soviet Pact was signed on _____ August 1939.
Match each event to its correct date.

flashcard_questions.a: A secret plan to give Mussolini most of Abyssinia to end the crisis; it leaked and caused a political scandal

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the League's sanctions against Italy fail over Abyssinia?
flashcard_questions.a: They excluded oil, coal, and steel — the resources Italy most needed for its military campaign

flashcard_questions.q: When did Germany remilitarise the Rhineland and why was it significant?
flashcard_questions.a: March 1936 — it violated both Versailles and Locarno but Britain and France took no military action
The union of Germany and Austria proclaimed by Hitler in March 1938, forbidden under Versailles

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Munich Agreement of September 1938 do?
flashcard_questions.a: Transferred the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia to Germany; Czechoslovakia was not consulted

flashcard_questions.q: What was Chamberlain's phrase after returning from Munich?
flashcard_questions.a: He claimed to have secured 'peace for our time'

flashcard_questions.q: What was the 'Guilty Men' view of appeasement?
flashcard_questions.a: That Chamberlain and his colleagues made disastrous and avoidable mistakes by trusting Hitler

flashcard_questions.q: What did the secret protocol of the Nazi-Soviet Pact contain?
flashcard_questions.a: A division of Eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence

flashcard_questions.q: When did Britain and France declare war on Germany?
flashcard_questions.a: 3 September 1939, two days after the German invasion of Poland

flashcard_questions.q: What is R.A.C. Parker's revisionist argument about appeasement?
flashcard_questions.a: That Chamberlain faced genuine constraints — incomplete rearmament, public hostility to war — and made defensible decisions given his information

glossary_terms.definition: An independent African kingdom, also known as Ethiopia, which Italy invaded in October 1935; the League imposed sanctions on Italy but they were too partial to be effective.
The union of Germany and Austria, proclaimed by Hitler in March 1938; it was forbidden under the Treaty of Versailles.

The agreement signed in September 1938 by Britain, France, Germany, and Italy that transferred the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia to Germany; often cited as the high point of the policy of appeasement.
The policy of making concessions to a potential aggressor in order to avoid war, most closely associated with British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain in the late 1930s.

A non-aggression pact signed between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union on 23 August 1939, which included a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence and cleared the way for Germany to invade Poland.

hero_image_caption: Chamberlain returns from Munich holding the agreement, September 1938
